subject: crested macaque
title: What If a Monkey Took a Selfie? Courts Spent Years Deciding Who Owned It

scenes.text: What if a monkey took a selfie? Then who owns the photo? Courts actually had to decide.
2011, Sulawesi, Indonesia. A wildlife photographer leaves his camera unattended. A crested macaque starts pressing the shutter.
The selfies become famous. Then, in 2015, an animal rights group sues on the monkey's behalf, claiming he owns the copyright.
The photographer agrees to give a quarter of his future earnings from the photos to charities protecting the monkeys.
In April 2018, a US appeals court rules: animals cannot sue under copyright law, because they are not human.
The monkey in the case was named Naruto. His species is critically endangered, and one selfie made it famous.

description:
What if a monkey took a selfie? In 2011, on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, a crested macaque picked up a wildlife photographer's unattended camera and pressed the shutter repeatedly.
In 2015 the animal rights group PETA sued in the monkey's name, Naruto, claiming he owned the copyright. The photographer agreed to donate 25 percent of his future earnings from the pictures to charities protecting crested macaques, and on 23 April 2018 the US Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that animals, not being human, cannot sue under the Copyright Act. The species is critically endangered.
